after.problem: Compute the arc length of $y=\frac{2}{3}{({x}^{2}+1)}^{3/2}$ for $x\in [1,4].$
after.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{2}{3}{({x}^{2}+1)}^{3/2},$ $a=1,$ and $b=4.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{({x}^{2}+1)}^{1/2}\cdot 2x=2x\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)}
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{[2x\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)}]}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+4{x}^{4}+4{x}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2{x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =2{x}^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}=2{x}^{2}+1$ to the formula for the arc length, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(2{x}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+x)|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =[\frac{2}{3}(4)^{3}+(4)]-[\frac{2}{3}(1)^{3}+(1)] \\  & =45.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2

Which of the following gives the length of the curve y=19(2x3+1)3/2 on [0,3]?

a
∫034x6+2x2+1dx
b
∫032x12+x4+1dx
c
∫032x7+x4+1dx
d
∫032x8+2x4+1dx
e
∫032x6+x2+1dx
Submit

decision.explanation: By the chain rule, y'=x^2\sqrt{2x^3+1}, so (y')^2=2x^7+x^4. The arc-length formula therefore gives L=\int_0^3\sqrt{1+(y')^2}\,dx=\int_0^3\sqrt{2x^7+x^4+1}\,dx, which is option c.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Which of the following gives the length of the curve $y=\frac{1}{9}{(2{x}^{3}+1)}^{3/2}$ on $[0,3]?$
after.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{1}{9}{(2{x}^{3}+1)}^{3/2},$ $a=0,$ and $b=3.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{9}(\frac{3}{2})6{x}^{2}{(2{x}^{3}+1)}^{1/2}={x}^{2}\sqrt{2{x}^{3}+1}
$$

Substituting ${f}^{′}(x)={x}^{2}\sqrt{2{x}^{3}+1}$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+{[{f}^{′}(x)]}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+{({x}^{2}\sqrt{2{x}^{3}+1})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}(2{x}^{3}+1)}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+2{x}^{7}+{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{2{x}^{7}+{x}^{4}+1}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Representation For an Arc Length
content.problem: Which of the following gives the length of the curve $y=\frac{1}{9}{(2{x}^{3}+1)}^{3/2}$ on $[0,3]?$
content.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{1}{9}{(2{x}^{3}+1)}^{3/2},$ $a=0,$ and $b=3.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{9}(\frac{3}{2})6{x}^{2}{(2{x}^{3}+1)}^{1/2}={x}^{2}\sqrt{2{x}^{3}+1}
$$

Substituting ${f}^{′}(x)={x}^{2}\sqrt{2{x}^{3}+1}$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+{[{f}^{′}(x)]}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+{({x}^{2}\sqrt{2{x}^{3}+1})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}(2{x}^{3}+1)}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+2{x}^{7}+{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{2{x}^{7}+{x}^{4}+1}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: The length of a curve $y=f(x)$ is given by ${\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.$ Which of the following could be  an equation for this curve?
after.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We're given that 

$$
L={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

$$
[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}=\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}\,⟹\,{f}^{′}(x)=\pm \frac{1}{1-x}.
$$

Integrating the above equation with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\pm \int \frac{1}{1-x}\text{ d}x \\  & =\pm (-\operatorname{ln}⁡|1-x|)+C \\  & =\pm \operatorname{ln}⁡(1-x)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

The length of a curve y=f(x) is given by ∫01/21+1(1−x)2dx. Which of the following could be an equation for this curve?

a
y=1(1−x)2
b
y=11−x+2
c
y=ln⁡(1−x)+7
d
y=ln⁡(x+1)−1
e
y=−11+x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The arc length of a curve y=f(x) between x=a and x=b can be found using the formula L=∫ab1+[f′(x)]2dx.

We're given that

L=∫01/21+1(1−x)2dx.

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

[f′(x)]2=1(1−x)2⟹f′(x)=±11−x.

Integrating the above equation with respect to x, we get

f(x)=±∫11−x dx=±(−ln⁡|1−x|)+C=±ln⁡(1−x)+C.

From the given options, the only one that has the required form is y=ln⁡(1−x)+7.

content.problem: The length of a curve $y=f(x)$ is given by ${\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.$ Which of the following could be  an equation for this curve?
content.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We're given that 

$$
L={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

$$
[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}=\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}\,⟹\,{f}^{′}(x)=\pm \frac{1}{1-x}.
$$

Integrating the above equation with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\pm \int \frac{1}{1-x}\text{ d}x \\  & =\pm (-\operatorname{ln}⁡|1-x|)+C \\  & =\pm \operatorname{ln}⁡(1-x)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given options, the only one that has the required form is $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-x)+7.$
